items.area: R2 — tracked in the backup service
items.description: R2: "The better solution would be to track this in the backup service. I feel like the end to end solution would be to add metadata to the upload indicating for how long it's valid (two days in our example). The backup service can then report that it didn't receive (and successfully upload) a backup within that period. For bonus points the check would actually read some JSON file from the backup server containing this metadata. I'm envisioning a .metadata.json file next to the backup, for now containing only this data field." Freshness is tracked in backup-server. Each upload declares how long it is valid. backup-server writes that to a .metadata.json file next to the backup, containing only the validity field, and reads those files back from cloud storage. It reports a stream that has received no successfully uploaded backup within the declared period.
items.rationale: Freshness is tracked in backup-server, not in its uploaders. `handleUpload` writes `<object>.metadata.json`, holding only `{"valid_for":"<duration>"}`, once the backup has landed; the freshness watcher lists every scope folder under the remote, reads each stream's newest declaring metadata file back with `rclone cat`, and publishes the stream's landing and valid-until times, so a stream with no backup inside its declared period is past its valid-until. The Go suite is green with `-race`, and the tests cover each edge through an in-memory backend. Live on prd, the new backup-server runs (image sha256:0ffa8be8…) and its first full read of the real Drive remote finished without error 21 s after start. Not yet proven against real Drive: writing a metadata file and reading it back. Only listing has run live, because no upload has declared a validity yet. The first ones are tonight's nightly runs, and V19 settles them.

items.description: An upload that declares a validity leaves <backup object name>.metadata.json next to the backup, holding only {"valid_for": "<duration>"}, written only after the backup has landed in cloud storage. The file is plain JSON that backup-server can read back (it holds only the age public key, decisions.md:100). A validity that is not a positive duration is refused before anything is stored. An upload that declares nothing behaves as before and writes no metadata; today's server reads only filename from the query (DockerImages backup-server/src/internal/handler/handler.go:76).
items.rationale: An upload with `valid_for` leaves `<object>.age.metadata.json` beside the backup, plain JSON holding only `{"valid_for":"<duration>"}`, written after the backup lands; a backup that fails writes none; a metadata write that fails deletes both and returns 500; a `valid_for` that is not a positive Go duration is refused with 400 before anything is stored; an upload that declares nothing writes no metadata. Proven by the handler tests over the in-memory backend and by reading the code. A real metadata file on Drive first exists tonight (V19).

items.description: A stream is scope + file name. Every scope folder under backup-server's remote that holds declaring backups is watched, whether or not the scope still has a credential, so a lost credential store or a removed credential leaves its streams watched. A stream stays watched while any of its kept backups declares a validity. It is overdue once its newest backup's landing time plus the newest declared validity has passed. A stream with no declaring backup is not watched. A stream whose backups have all been pruned stops being watched, and its alert clears. An uploader that stops declaring keeps its stream watched.
items.rationale: A stream is scope plus file name, and the watched set comes from Drive, never from the credential store: `freshness.New` is given only the backend and the remote, and `Refresh` walks `ListDirs(remote)`. A stream stays watched while any kept backup has a metadata file, is valid until its newest backup's stamp plus the newest declaring backup's validity, drops out when its backups are all pruned, and is not watched with no declaring backup. Each edge has a named test.
evidence: go: `cexec go sh -c 'cd /work/DockerImages/backup-server/src && gofmt -l . ; go vet ./... ; go test -race -count=1 ./...'` on go1.26.5 (test phase r1, 2026-09-19): gofmt and vet print nothing; ok for auth, freshness, handler and pipeline

items.description: Pruning counts backups only: a scope keeps its newest `retention` backups regardless of how many metadata files sit beside them. Each pruned backup's metadata file is deleted with it. Today prune counts every name in the scope (DockerImages backup-server/src/internal/pipeline/prune.go:14-41).
items.rationale: `Prune` splits a scope's names into backups and metadata files, keeps the newest `retention` backups, and deletes every other backup and every metadata file whose backup is not kept, including one whose backup is already gone. Metadata files never count toward retention.

items.description: A second critical alert fires when Prometheus cannot scrape backup-server, including when the target is gone entirely, or when backup-server cannot read cloud storage. It waits out a grace period, so a redeploy or a cloud-storage hiccup that clears by itself never pages; it fires once the watching has really been blind for hours.
items.rationale: `BackupWatcherBlind` is critical and fires when the newest successful full read any scrape in the last 6 h reported is over 6 h old, or when the series is absent for 6 h, so a target that is down, crash-looping or gone altogether, and a server whose reads fail, all fire only after hours; a redeploy or a self-clearing hiccup does not. The tests walk redeploys, failed reads, a gone target and a crash loop minute by minute. items.description: A refresh's Drive reads are bounded. A refresh lists each scope folder once and reads only metadata files it has not seen before; a metadata file, which never changes once written, is read once and remembered. A normal night costs a handful of Drive calls, not a re-read of every kept metadata file after each Postgres upload. Drive's per-minute query quota has already failed a backup mid-upload (DockerImages backup-server/src/internal/pipeline/backend.go:34-38), and the Postgres job uploads its databases one after another in the same window (HelmCharts charts/postgres-pas/templates/backup-configmap.yaml:57-64).
items.rationale: A refresh lists each scope folder once and reads only metadata files it has not read before. It reads only each stream's newest declaring file, remembered per scope, so a cold start reads one file per stream, a later refresh none, and an upload's refresh one and lists only its own scope. A named test pins each count. Live, the whole remote was read in 21 s with no metadata reads yet; tonight's runs put the real call counts through Drive (V19).
